prohibited_recommendations: Do not prescribe benzodiazepines for anxiety/agitation — they precipitate and prolong HE (use haloperidol or non-pharmacologic measures for agitation).
Do not prescribe sedating opioids — they worsen HE; consider acetaminophen at hepatic-safe dosing for pain.
Do not perform LP before neuroimaging excludes mass effect when the patient has altered mental status.
Hold propranolol during active hemorrhage with hypotension — blunts compensatory tachycardia.
Do not give NSAIDs (renal failure risk in cirrhosis).
Do not start protein restriction — outdated and harms outcomes.
Do not transfuse aggressively to normal Hgb — increases portal pressure and rebleeding.
required_recommendations: Urgent upper endoscopy with variceal banding — definitive control of nitrogen-load source.
Transfuse PRBC to target Hgb 7-8 g/dL (over-transfusion worsens portal pressures).
Empiric IV ceftriaxone 2 g daily for SBP + bleeding cirrhotic antibiotic prophylaxis; IV albumin 1.5 g/kg day 1, 1 g/kg day 3.
Lactulose enemas q4-6h until oral route safe (300 mL retention enema); add rifaximin 550 mg BID via NG.
IV thiamine 500 mg before any dextrose.
Airway management: intubate if grade IV / GCS <8; aspiration risk extremely high.

avoided_actions.rationale: Amyloid PET has no role in HE workup; reversible metabolic encephalopathy is the issue, not Alzheimer pathology.
DaTscan has no role in HE workup; the question is metabolic encephalopathy, not nigrostriatal degeneration.
Early-onset AD genetic panel has no role in HE workup; reversible metabolic encephalopathy is the diagnosis under consideration.

accepted: Hepatic encephalopathy (West Haven grade III-IV), alcoholic cirrhosis (Child-Pugh C, MELD 22) — precipitated by acute upper GI variceal hemorrhage (nitrogen load) plus spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (ascitic PMN 342) plus acute alcohol ingestion (ethanol 168).

differential.key_features: PMN 342, E. coli; treat empirically with ceftriaxone + albumin.
Coagulopathy + likely fall — CT head mandatory and excludes.
Ethanol 168 mg/dL contributes; tolerant alcoholic so cannot fully account for GCS 10; monitor for withdrawal 24-72 h post-stop.
Cr 1.8; reassess after volume/albumin; AKI affects ammonia clearance.
High thiamine-deficiency risk; give empiric thiamine before any dextrose.

key_clinical_evidence: HE is a clinical diagnosis: West Haven grading + evidence of liver dysfunction + exclusion of other causes of AMS — ammonia level is supportive only and correlates poorly with grade (AASLD 2014).

Precipitant identification is more actionable than the ammonia number: infection (SBP especially), GI bleed, electrolyte disturbance (hypokalemia/hyponatremia), constipation, sedative/CNS-depressant use, dehydration, dietary protein load, renal failure.
Upper GI bleed is one of the most potent HE precipitants — blood in gut is a massive nitrogen load; BUN/Cr ratio elevation supports an upper source.
SBP and variceal bleed coexist in roughly a third of severe HE cases — both must be addressed simultaneously.
Restrictive transfusion strategy (Hgb 7-8) reduces rebleeding in variceal hemorrhage.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Ethanol 168 cannot cause grade III-IV obtundation in a tolerant alcoholic; ammonia 187 + SBP + GI bleed + triphasic-wave EEG confirm HE.
red_herrings.intended_effect: Attribute GCS 10 entirely to alcohol intoxication and observe.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Diagnostic paracentesis is safe in Child-Pugh C with coagulopathy; prophylactic FFP/platelets are not required per AASLD.

patient.history_present_illness: Mr. W. is a 58-year-old man with severe alcoholic cirrhosis (Child-Pugh C, MELD 22) who was found confused and combative in his home by his adult son, who called 911. He could not be aroused to follow commands and had large amounts of tarry black stool on his clothing. His son found empty vodka bottles — the patient had been drinking. On presentation, he is hypotensive (BP 96/58), tachycardic (HR 124), and febrile (37.8°C). He has prominent jaundice, caput medusae, large-volume ascites, fetor hepaticus, and bilateral spider angiomata. Melena on rectal exam confirms active upper GI bleed. His neurological exam shows GCS 10 with prominent asterixis, disorientation, and bilateral Babinski signs. His ammonia is 187 µmol/L — markedly elevated.

neurological_exam.additional: Jaundice visible — sclerae and skin yellow. Spider angiomata on chest and shoulders. Caput medusae. Large-volume ascites. Fetor hepaticus — notable on entering room. Melena on rectal exam — active GI bleed.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Pupils 4 mm, equal, sluggishly reactive. Extraocular movements intact. Gag reflex diminished.
neurological_exam.gait: Unable to ambulate — too confused and uncooperative.
neurological_exam.mental_status: GCS 10 (E2V3M5). Confused and combative. Responds to voice with incomprehensible sounds. Localizes pain. Asterixis prominent bilaterally on arm extension. Disoriented — unable to state name correctly. Cannot follow any commands reliably.
neurological_exam.motor: Moving all extremities spontaneously. Tone increased. Occasional myoclonic jerks bilateral hands.
